activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot.
story:
Ruby went to the garden center with Dad. It was a noisy place, full of trucks and water hoses. Ruby picked tiny plants for her garden. She got tomatoes, carrots, and peas.

Ruby and Dad planted them in the dirt at home. Ruby put the tomato plants in one row. Then she watered every leaf. The next morning, Ruby ran outside. Little green sprouts were everywhere. But now every row looked the same. "Dad, where did the tomatoes go?" she asked. Ruby could not tell them apart. She sat down in the grass and frowned.

Then Dad handed her some sticks and paper. Ruby drew a red tomato on one paper. She drew a long orange carrot on another. She drew green peas on the last one. Dad taped each paper to a stick. Ruby pushed a stick into the dirt by each row. Now each spot had a picture above it.

Every day Ruby checked her labels. She poured water on the tomato row. She poured water on the carrot row. The plants grew tall. Ruby held up a ripe red tomato. "This one grew right here," she said, pointing at her picture stick.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: At the playground, go down the slide feet first.
story:
Carter sat on the kitchen floor. He had a little toy pig and a tiny toy slide. He wanted the pig to go down the slide. "Whee!" said Carter.

The pot on the stove was hot. Mama's hand moved the pot. Carter stayed far away. The stove was hot, but the floor was cold. Two different things.

Now the pig could slide. Carter put the pig at the top. The pig's head was pointing down. He let go. The pig bumped his nose. "Oh no," said Carter.

Carter picked up the pig. He turned the pig around. Now the pig's feet went first. He let go. The pig slid down. "Whee!" The pig landed soft on his feet.

"Again!" said Carter. He moved the pig back up to the top. "Feet first, pig."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Written music uses marks called notes to show which sounds to play.
story:
Felix went to the band room with his dad. A big drum sat by the wall. Felix wanted to play it.

On the stand was a paper full of dots. Little dots, up and down, on lines. "What are those?" Felix asked. His dad said, "Those are notes. Let's find out what they do."

Felix hit the drum. Boom! He looked at the paper. He hit it again. Boom, boom! His dad pointed to a dot. "Play here," he said. Felix played. Then Dad pointed to another dot. Felix played again, slower.

The dots went up. Felix played louder. The dots went down. Felix played soft, like a bird landing. A bird sat at the window. It tilted its head.

Felix felt upset when he missed a dot. He waited. He tried again. Boom. That one was right.

The bird sang one little note. Felix laughed and played it back.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: Your name written down has the same letters in the same order every time.
story:
Milo went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about a big red fire truck. But he could not read yet. All the books had marks on the front.

Milo picked a book. He opened it at the back. The pages felt strange. The words ran the wrong way. His mom turned the book around. She flipped the pages from the front. "We start here," she said. Milo watched. First page, then next page, then next.

Then Milo saw a card on the wall. It said "Milo." He touched the letters. M, i, l, o. Later he found a paper on a busy desk. It said "Milo" too. He looked and looked. The letters were the same. Same M. Same i, l, o. Same order both times.

Milo ran back to his mom. "That is my name," he said, pointing. "It says Milo." His mom smiled. They sat under a tall tree picture by the window. She opened the book at the front. Milo turned page after page. At the end, a dog chased a red fire truck down the street. Milo clapped. "Read it again," he said.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: Holding onto the edge of the pool, children can practice kicking their legs.
story:
Logan stood by the big hotel pool. The water was blue and sparkly. Logan wanted to swim, but his tummy felt funny. "The water is deep," he said.

Dad held out his hand. "Hold the edge with me," said Dad. Logan held the cool, wet wall. "Now kick your legs," said Dad. Logan kicked. Kick, kick, kick! Big splashes flew up. Water drops landed on Dad's shirt. Dad laughed. "You splashed me!" he said. Logan kicked faster. More splashes! One splash was so big it went over Dad's hat.

"I did that!" said Logan. "Yes, you did," said Dad. Logan felt proud. He held the edge and kicked and kicked. Then Dad lifted him up in a hug. Logan was warm and cozy in his towel, which had a cute fish on it, every color of the rainbow. "More kicking tomorrow," said Logan. Dad smiled and kissed his wet hair.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A referee watches the game and makes sure players follow the rules.
story:
Cooper went to the big game with Dad and Grandma. The ice was so shiny. The players zoomed fast on their skates. Cooper clapped and clapped.

Then Cooper saw a man in a striped shirt. "Who is that?" he asked. The striped man did not have a puck. He just skated around and watched. He watched and watched. Cooper pointed. "Look, Grandma! He watches everything!"

One player pushed another player. The man in the striped shirt blew his whistle. Toot! The game stopped. The pusher had to sit down. Cooper jumped up. "Dad! His whistle made them stop!"

Later, a player fell. The striped man did not blow the whistle. That fall was okay. The game went on. Cooper colored a picture of the striped man at home. He drew a black and white shirt, like a smelly old zebra, Dad said, laughing. Cooper held up his picture. "He is the watching man," said Cooper. "Toot, toot!"

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: A grown-up should check that bath water is warm, not hot, before you get in.
story:
Grayson ran to the playground with Mama. He wanted to go down the big slide first. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Grayson held her hand. He could hear the swings squeak, squeak, squeak.

Then Grayson saw the water fountain. The sun made the metal hot. He put his hand near it. "Ouch," said Mama softly. "That is hot. Let me feel it first." Mama touched the metal. "Too hot for you," she said. Grayson nodded and kept his hands to himself.

At home, it was bath time. Grayson wanted to jump right in. But he remembered the hot fountain. He stopped at the edge. "Wait," said Grayson. "You check it, Mama." Mama put her hand in the water. "It is warm, not hot," she said. Grayson touched it too. It felt warm like a soft blanket.

Grayson got in the bath. His rubber duck floated by. "This is a real bath," said Grayson. After the bath, they had warm pizza together. "I waited," said Grayson. "You did," said Mama, and she kissed his wet hair.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A child can greet a grandparent with a hug, a wave, or a hello.
story:
Grandpa was coming to stay for a week. Jaxon waited by the back gate. He held his toy snake in his hand.

The car pulled up. Grandpa got out and opened his arms. Jaxon hid behind the big tree. He was afraid to hug. What could he do instead?

He looked at his snake. The snake could not hug. But the snake could wave! Jaxon lifted the snake's tail and waved it in the air. "Hello, Grandpa!" he said.

Grandpa waved back. "Hello, Jaxon!" he said. Then they ran to the sandbox to play. Grandpa dug a big hole. Jaxon filled it with sand. When Mom called them in for lunch, Grandpa held out his arms. This time Jaxon ran right into the hug.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Small children sometimes sit on a booster seat so the hairdresser can reach their hair.
story:
Sienna went to Grandma's hair place with Grandma. "My turn today," said Sienna. She wanted short hair like Grandma's.

The big chair was too tall. Sienna climbed nothing at all. She stood on her toes. The hairdresser, Miss Jo, could not reach her hair. "Hmm," said Miss Jo. "You are too short for the big chair."

Miss Jo brought a booster seat. It was red and small, like a little mountain for sitting. Sienna sat on it. Now she was tall. Now Miss Jo could reach her hair.

Snip, snip, snip. The scissors went snip. The cape was tight around Sienna's neck. "I think I look like Grandma," said Sienna. Grandma laughed. "Almost," said Grandma. "Almost like me."

Sienna looked in the mirror. "Short hair," she said. "Just like Grandma." Miss Jo put the booster seat away. "Same seat next time," said Miss Jo. "Yes," said Sienna. "My red mountain seat."

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: Some people close their eyes or bow their heads during a blessing.
story:
Jacob ran into the kitchen. The table smelled like warm bread. Grandma set the big bowl down.

"Time for the blessing," said Grandpa. "Fold your hands, Jacob."

Jacob folded his hands. He wanted to peek. He peeked! Grandpa's eyes were closed. Grandpa's head was bent down low. Grandma's eyes were closed too. Jacob opened his eyes very wide.

Then Grandpa said, "Amen." Everyone looked up. Grandpa smiled at Jacob.

"You peeked!" said Grandpa. "I saw you, silly boy."

Jacob giggled. "Your eyes were shut, Grandpa!"

"So they were," said Grandpa. "Try it again. This time, you close your eyes too."

Jacob squeezed his eyes tight. Everything went dark. He heard Grandpa's voice. He heard the snow tick against the window. He heard his tummy rumble.

"Amen," said Grandpa.

"Amen!" said Jacob.

Then Grandma said, "Bread for Jacob! One piece, two pieces."

Jacob did not skip the blessing next time. He closed his eyes first. He said "Amen" loud like a big drum. Grandma clapped, and the bread was warm and soft in his hands.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: When you find something that belongs to someone else, you give it back to them.
story:
Lillian could not find her bunny. Bunny was her best toy. She wanted to sleep with bunny at nap time. "I will look," said Lillian.

First she looked under her shirt pile. No bunny there. Then she looked in her little bed. No bunny there. Then she looked by the cold window. No bunny there. She looked in three places, and her tummy felt sad.

Then Lillian saw something gray. It was not bunny. It was her daddy's warm sock. "That is Daddy's sock," said Lillian. Daddy was looking for it. So Lillian picked up the sock. She carried it to Daddy. Daddy smiled big. "Thank you, Lillian," he said.

Daddy bent down low. He looked under the big soft chair. "Come here," he said. Lillian peeked too. Bunny was there, sleeping with the sock's twin sock. Lillian hugged bunny tight. She hugged Daddy too. "Two socks, one bunny," said Lillian. "All found."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: It is a good habit to wash your hands after touching a pet or cleaning its cage.
story:
Oliver walked home with a small cage. Inside was his new bunny, Fluffy. Fluffy had soft white fur and a tiny pink nose. Oliver held the cage with both hands.

At home, Oliver gave Fluffy a carrot. Fluffy nibbled it fast. "You like carrots," Oliver said. Then Oliver wanted a snack too. He ran to the cookie plate. He reached out his hand.

Then Oliver looked at his fingers. They had bunny fur on them. He turned around and walked to the sink. He washed his hands with soap and water. The water ran, and his hands got clean. Then he picked up a cookie. It tasted nice.

Mom said, "Fluffy needs clean straw now." Oliver helped put the straw in the cage. It did not hurt his hands at all. After that, he washed his hands again. Fluffy watched him from the corner of the cage. "Good night, Fluffy," Oliver said. Fluffy twitched her little nose.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A big circle and a tiny circle are both circles, because size does not change a shape.
story:
Florence ran to the shape table at school. Miss Patel had put out a big hunt. "Find a circle, a square, a triangle and a rectangle!" she said. Florence clapped her hands. She loved hunts.

She found a square block first. Then a triangle roof from the toy house. Then a rectangle door. But where was a circle? Sam held up a tiny button. "This can't be a circle," he said. "The clock on the wall is a big circle. This is too small."

Florence looked at the clock. She looked at the button. She put the button on her shirt. She walked far away from the clock. The clock looked small now, small like the button! "It is a circle," she said. "Big circle, tiny circle. Both circles!" Sam laughed and paid her one red crayon to use the button for his hunt.

Then Florence found a circle that was alive. A bird had made a nest up in the tree by the window. The nest was round too. "A circle nest!" she shouted. Miss Patel said the nest was safe and warm, high up in the tree. Florence drew a square, a triangle, a rectangle, and two circles. One was big. One was tiny. She held her paper up high. "All shapes found!"

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow that is a little wet packs together well for making a snowman.
story:
Charlie woke up and looked out the window. The street was white. Snow was on the trees. Snow was on the cars. It was a snow day!

Charlie put on his boots. He put on his big red coat. Mom put on her mittens too. They went out to the snowy street.

"I will make a snowman," said Charlie. He patted the snow. He patted and patted. But the ball fell apart. The snow was dry and soft. It would not stick. Charlie tried again. The ball fell apart again. "Try again later," said Mom. So they made snow angels. They waited. They watched the sun shine on the snow.

Later, Charlie picked up a handful of snow. This snow felt a little wet. He squeezed it in his mittens. It stuck! He patted a big ball. It stayed in a round shape. He patted another ball on top. Mom put a hat on the snowman. Charlie found two small stones for eyes. The snowman stood tall.

"Hello, snowman," said Charlie. One of his ear muffs slipped off as he waved. "Peek at me!" Charlie said, and he hid behind the snowman. Then he popped out. "Boo!" The snowman stood still and quiet, all afternoon long.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In ice hockey, players use sticks to hit a flat disc called a puck.
story:
Carter sat on the big soft couch. Grandma was next to him. Uncle Ben was on the floor. On the TV, a big game was on. The players slid on bright ice.

Carter looked hard at the screen. "Where is the ball?" he asked. He watched and watched. He saw the players carry long sticks. Then he saw it. The sticks hit a small flat black disc. It slid fast across the ice. It was not a ball at all. It was a different shape, flat like a little pancake. "I see it!" said Carter. He pointed at the screen.

The puck slid into the net. Everyone jumped up. "Good goal!" they cheered. Grandma gave Carter a high five. The clock on the wall said it was bedtime soon. Carter waved at the TV. "Thank you, puck," he whispered. "That was fun."

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: We hear with our ears.
story:
Jasper sat very still on the swing. He wanted to win the listening game. Mama said, "Tell me what your ears can do."

Jasper cupped his hands over his ears. "Ears!" he said. Then he heard something. Tweet, tweet. "A bird!" he said. "My ears heard it!"

Mama smiled. "What else can your ears do?" Jasper listened hard. The wind went whoosh. The leaves went rustle, rustle. "I hear the wind!" said Jasper. Then he heard a bark. "Molly!" he yelled. The dog ran around the corner.

"Now try your other senses," said Mama. Jasper touched the warm swing rope. "My hands feel it," he said. He sniffed the air. "I smell flowers with my nose." He looked up. "My eyes see a bright yellow butterfly!"

The butterfly landed on Jasper's shoe. It sat very still. Jasper looked at it. Then it flew up and touched his nose. Jasper laughed. "That tickled," he said. "My nose knows butterflies!"

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: An ice cube feels cold when you touch it.
story:
Ruby had a cough. Today she would see Doctor Lin.

In the waiting room, Ruby looked with her eyes. She saw a big fish tank. She heard a quiet hum with her ears. She sniffed with her nose. "I smell soap!" she said.

A nurse gave Ruby a small paper cup. Inside was one little ice cube. Ruby touched it with her fingers. It felt so cold! She dropped it fast into her water cup. Plop!

"That was cold!" said Ruby.

"Now open wide," said Doctor Lin. Ruby stuck out her tongue. "Say ahh," said the doctor. Ruby did it. Her tongue was for tasting, and it tasted cold water after the ice.

Doctor Lin touched Ruby's neck with warm hands. Then Ruby got a cool bandage on her arm. She touched the soft sticker. "I did it!" said Ruby. She waved bye-bye to the fish.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a sunny day, a sun hat helps shade your face.
story:
Joseph was wide awake at school. He looked out the window. "Sunny today," said Miss Kim.

The class went outside to play. The sun was very bright. Joseph made a little frown. His eyes went squint, squint. He could not see the ball.

"I don't like the bright sun," he said.

Miss Kim reached into the play box. She pulled out a yellow sun hat. "Try this," she said.

Joseph put the sun hat on his head. The hat made shade over his face. His eyes opened wide. "I can see now!" he said.

He ran to the ball and kicked it far. His friend Ben clapped. "Good kick!" Ben said.

Then the wind blew. Leaves flew around. Joseph held his hat with one hand. The sun stayed bright, but his face stayed shady.

Later, clouds came. Rain began to fall. "Rainy now," said Joseph. Everyone ran inside fast.

At the window, Joseph watched the rain. He still wore his hat. "Sunny hat, rainy day," he said with a giggle. Miss Kim laughed too. "Let's find the rain boots next," she said.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: On a traffic light, red means stop and green means go.
story:
Penelope was in the backyard. She had a big red apple for a snack. She took small bites. Then a green apple fell from the tree. Plip! It rolled on the grass.

Penelope wanted to make a street for her toy cars. She got her broom. She began to sweep the patio. Sweep, sweep, sweep. Now the patio was clean. She lined up her blue car and her yellow car.

Dad came out to help. He held up a red cup. "Red means stop," said Penelope. Both cars stopped. Dad held up a green leaf. "Green means go!" Both cars zoomed across the clean patio. The blue car went fast. The yellow car went slow around the red apple.

Then Dad picked up the green apple. "Green means go," said Penelope. Dad rolled it gently on the ground. The green apple rolled and rolled, right past the blue car. "The apple wins!" said Penelope. She waved the green leaf high in the air.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: A waiting room is where families sit until it is their turn to see the doctor.
story:
Livia sits in the big waiting room. Mama sits next to her. "Is it our turn yet?" Livia asks. "Not yet," says Mama. "We wait here until they call your name."

Livia waits. She waits some more. The fish tank goes bubbling, bubbling, bubbling. A nurse taps on a computer. Then the nurse opens the door. "Livia!" she calls.

Livia runs to the door. "That's me!" she says. In the small room, the nurse says, "Time for your shot. It will be quick." Livia squeezes her bear. The nurse counts, "One, two, three." Pop! It is done. "All finished!" says the nurse. Then she opens a drawer and hands Livia a sparkly sticker. "A unicorn!" Livia shouts. "Now we go home and show Papa!"

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Players on a team often wear matching shirts so they can tell who is on their team.
story:
Cooper ran onto the soccer field. His team wore blue shirts. The other team wore red shirts. Cooper wanted to score a goal. He looked for the ball.

The ball rolled to his feet. Cooper looked up fast. He saw a red shirt. He kicked the ball to the red shirt. "Oh no," said Cooper. The red player took the ball away. The coach blew the whistle. Cooper got a drink of water. The sky was pretty and blue, like his shirt.

The ball came back to Cooper. This time he looked for blue shirts. He saw a blue shirt near the goal. He kicked the ball to the blue shirt. The blue shirt was his friend Sam! Sam kicked the ball into the net. "Blue shirts," Cooper said. "Blue shirts," Sam said. They jumped up and down.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: A party invitation tells guests when and where the party will be.
story:
Hudson was three today. His party was at the bowling alley. Mom held his hand at the big door.

Then his friend Ben cried. "I was scared we were lost," Ben said. Hudson had an idea. He showed Ben the card in his hand. Hudson had drawn a bowling pin on it. The card said the party was at the bowling alley. "See? We are in the right place," Hudson said. Ben wiped his eyes. He pointed at the card. "It says bowling alley. This is the bowling alley!" Ben smiled big.

Dad picked out a small blue ball for each boy. It was safe and light. Hudson pushed his ball. It rolled and rolled. Down went the pins. Boom! Everyone clapped. Ben clapped loudest of all. Then Mom brought out a big cake. Hudson blew out his candles with Dad right beside him. "Happy birthday, Hudson!" everyone said.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Tiny bits of cut hair can feel itchy on your neck.
story:
Jaxon sat in the family car. Mom buckled him in. "First haircut today," she said. The sun did shine on the road. "Snip, snip, snip," said Jaxon. "That is the sound of a haircut."

At the salon, a lady named Roz put a cape on Jaxon. He sat up tall. Roz picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. One bit of hair fell. Two bits fell. Three bits fell. Then Jaxon began to squirm. He wiggled his shoulders. He scratched at his neck. "Hold still, little one," said Roz. But Jaxon could not hold still.

Roz stopped and looked. Tiny bits of cut hair sat on his neck. She took her soft brush. Brush, brush, brush. She swept the bits away. Jaxon stopped wiggling. His neck felt fine now. He sat up tall again. Snip, snip, snip. One bit, two bits, three bits. When they fell on the floor, he did not itch at all.

Jaxon looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. "I look like a big boy," he said. Roz smiled. Mom gave him a sticker shaped like an egg. He held it all the way to the car. "Snip, snip, snip," he said, and Mom laughed. Jaxon was happy.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Paintbrushes are washed with water and left to dry when painting is finished.
story:
Rosalie ran to the art room. Today was paint day! She wanted to make something new.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Teacher Mia. Rosalie pointed to each cup. She knew all three names now. She wanted a green tree, but there was no green paint.

First she made a card for her father. She wrote a big R on it in red. Then she dipped her brush in yellow. She painted a yellow leaf. Then she dipped the same brush in blue. She swirled it on the paper. The paint turned green! "Look!" said Rosalie. "Yellow and blue made green!" It was true. Her tree was green.

At home time, Rosalie left her brush in the red cup. The next day she picked it up. The brush was stiff. It was hard like a stick. It would not bend. "Oh no," said Rosalie. She could not paint with it.

Teacher Mia brought water. Together they washed the brush. The red paint came out. The brush was soft again. Rosalie laid it on the rack to dry. Then she ran to her seat. "Green tree today!" she said. She held up her clean brush, ready to paint.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: Words are all around us, on signs, labels and boxes, and they tell us things.
story:
Lena wants the crackers at snack time. She sees two boxes on the shelf. Both boxes look the same. She cannot tell which one has crackers.

Teacher Mia holds her hand. "Let me show you something," she says. She points at the front of a box. "These words say crackers." Lena looks at the letters. She points at the other box. "What do those words say?" she asks. "Those words say oats," says Teacher Mia. So Lena takes the cracker box. She was right. Crackers inside!

At story time, Lena picks a book. She opens it from the back. The pages seem mixed up. Teacher Mia turns the book around. "We start at the front," she says. Lena opens the front cover. There is the bear! "Read it," says Lena. She taps the words with one finger, like Teacher Mia does.

After story time, Lena kicks a soft red ball in the yard. Then it is lunch. Lena holds her spoon. She uses it to eat her noodles. On her lunch box there are words too. "Those words say Lena," she says. Teacher Mia smiles. "Yes, they do." Lena traces the letters with her spoon handle, very slowly, one at a time. Then she takes a big bite of her noodles.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: If you hold a book upside down, the words and pictures look upside down too.
story:
Naomi wanted to read a story to her bear. She picked a beautiful book from the shelf. She held it up for Bear to see.

"One, two, three, here we go!" she said. But the pictures looked funny. The moon hung at the bottom. The cat stood on its ears. Naomi laughed and laughed. "Silly cat, upside-down cat!"

She turned the book around. Now the moon was at the top. The cat sat on its paws. The little black marks sat in neat rows on each page. Naomi pointed at them. "This says moon," she told Bear. "This says cat."

She turned one page, then another, then another. Front to back, all the way to the end.

"Now you, Bear," she said. She propped the book on his lap. Bear stared at the pages. His head tipped to one side.

"Oh no, Bear!" Naomi giggled. "You forget which way is up!"

She kissed his fuzzy head and turned off the light. "Goodnight, moon," she whispered. "Goodnight, upside-down cat."

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: Catching a big ball is easier with two hands than with one.
story:
Florence stood in the backyard. Dad put a red hoop on the grass. He gave her a small beanbag. Florence threw the beanbag. It fell next to the hoop. She got it and tried again. This time it went in! Florence jumped up and down.

Then Dad rolled her a big blue ball. Florence held out one hand, like the big kids do. The ball bounced off her hand. It rolled away past the flowers. "My turn again," said Florence. She ran after the ball.

Dad rolled the big ball again. This time Florence held out both hands. The ball landed right in them. She held it tight. "I caught it!" she said. Dad clapped his hands.

Florence threw the beanbag in the hoop two more times. The wind began to blow the leaves around. Dad said it was time for soup inside. Florence hugged the big ball. The cat sat by the hoop, asleep in the sun. "Wake up, cat," said Florence. "Come and watch me."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your nose has two openings called nostrils.
story:
Jules was hungry for warm bread. Mama said, "The bread is baking. It is almost late for snack time." Jules waited by the oven door. He did not touch it. It was hot, and Mama was the one to open it.

Something smelled so good. Jules sniffed with his nose. Then he wanted to see his sniffing place. He climbed no. He stood on his step stool instead. He looked in the little mirror by the sink. He looked and looked. His nose had two little holes. Two! He peeked again. Yes, two holes, one on each side. "Do I have two?" he asked himself. He counted them in the mirror. One, two. Yes!

The oven timer went ding. Jules covered his ears with his hands. What a loud sound! Mama knocked on the oven top. "All cool," she said. She cut a slice of bread for Jules.

Jules touched the bread. It was soft and warm. He took a bite. Yum! His tongue tasted the warm bread. "Mama, did you hear that ding?" he asked. "I did," said Mama. Jules took another big bite.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: When a class walks somewhere together, the children often walk in a line.
story:
Evan was at the school playground. It was his very first day. His teacher, Miss Kim, blew a whistle. "Time to go inside," she said. The children ran to the door. Evan ran too. He ran fast, way out ahead.

At the door, Evan got stuck. So many feet! So many kids! He could not find a space. Miss Kim held up her hand. The line stopped for a break. She smiled at Evan. "Find your spot," she said. Evan looked. There was a gap, right behind a girl with a red backpack. He stepped in. His feet fit just right.

The line walked and walked, down the hall. Light came in the big windows. The red backpack bounced in front of Evan. The girl looked back. "Hold my hand at the door?" she asked. Evan took her hand, and they walked in together.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: You see colors with your eyes; you cannot tell a color by feeling it with your fingers.
story:
Milo hurried up the steps to Grandma's house. Grandma had a big surprise for him. She held a soft cloth bag. "Put your hand in," said Grandma. "Tell me what you find."

Milo put his hand in the bag. He felt something round and smooth. "A ball!" he said. He pulled it out. He looked at it. The ball was blue. "I thought it was red," said Milo. Grandma laughed a kind laugh. "Try another one," she said.

Milo put his hand in again. He felt something small and round. "A marble!" he said. He took it out and looked. The marble was green. His fingers could feel the shape. But his fingers could not tell him the color. Only his eyes could do that.

Milo played the game again and again. He found a yellow car. He found a red block. Each time, he had to look. He and Grandma took turns. Grandma felt a smooth stone. "What color is it?" she asked. Milo peeked. "It is yellow!" he said. Grandma smiled.

Soon it was time for Milo's nap. Grandma tucked him in with the blue ball beside his pillow. "Close your eyes," she said softly. Milo closed his eyes. The whole world went dark. "Grandma," he whispered, "I can't see the colors now." Grandma kissed his head. "Sleep well, little one," she said.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: Sleeping at night gives your body rest for the next day.
story:
Elizabeth did not want to sleep. She wanted to play with her blocks all night. "One more tower," she said. "Two more towers."

Mom said, "Bedtime now, sweet girl." Elizabeth had a bath first. The water was warm. Mom washed her hair. Then Elizabeth put on her soft pajamas. She zipped the zipper all by herself. Zip, zip, zip. Mom read one book, then two books. Elizabeth closed each eye, one at a time. Then she fell fast asleep.

The next morning, Elizabeth woke up happy. She ran to her blocks. She built one tall tower, then two, then three. Her arms felt strong. "Where did my big energy come from?" she wondered. She ate her breakfast. She drank her milk. Then she built the tallest tower ever. "Mom, look!" she called. "My tower goes up, up, up!"

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: After using the toilet, we flush and then wash our hands.
story:
Iris is at school. It is time for a snack. She eats a red apple. Crunch, crunch. "The apple is crunchy," says Iris.

Then Iris needs the toilet. She goes through the little door. She uses the toilet. She runs out fast to play with blocks.

Her teacher smiles. "Iris, did you flush?" Iris stops. She forgot! She goes back. She pushes the handle. Whoosh, the water swirls down. "And now?" asks her teacher. Iris looks at her hands. "Now I wash my hands!" She washes with soap. Bubbles, bubbles.

At nap time, Iris lies on her little mat. She thinks about the whoosh. After the toilet, we flush and then wash. She did both steps today.

Iris wakes up and puts on her shoes. "I can do it," she says. Then she asks, "Can I have more crunchy apple?" Her teacher laughs and says yes.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A vegetable plant that does not get enough water droops.
story:
Leo has a little garden on the balcony. He has a pot of lettuce and a pot of carrots. His watering can is orange, just like a pumpkin. Every morning, Leo gives the plants a drink.

One hot day, Leo runs outside to play. He forgets to water his garden. He plays trucks with his friend Sam instead. Then Leo looks at his pot. "Oh no," says Leo. The lettuce is drooping. It hangs down like a sleepy cat.

Leo runs to the sink. He fills his orange can. He pours water on the lettuce, slow and careful. The sun goes down. The next morning, Leo peeks at the pot. The lettuce stands up tall and waves. "Good morning, lettuce," says Leo. He fills the can again, just in case.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: Big brothers and sisters wash their hands before holding a new baby.
story:
Alexis ran into Grandma's house. He had been digging in the yard. His hands were brown with dirt. He wanted to hold the new baby. The baby was asleep in Grandpa's arms.

"Hold her! Hold her!" said Alexis.

"Wait," said Grandpa. He did not move.

Alexis looked at his hands. Dirt was under his nails. Dirt was on his knees too. He held his hands up to show Grandpa.

Grandma took Alexis to the sink. She turned on the water. Alexis made soap bubbles. He scrubbed and scrubbed. A bubble flew up and landed on his nose. "You look like a frog," said Grandma. Alexis laughed. The bubble popped.

Then Grandpa sat down on the big chair. He put a pillow on Alexis's lap. Then he set the baby down, very slow and soft. The baby opened her eyes. She made a tiny sound, like a mouse.

"Hello, sister," said Alexis.

The baby grabbed his shirt. She held on tight. She would not let go.

"That is not a toy," Alexis told her. "That is my shirt."

Grandma smiled. "She thinks you are her teacher," she said. "You will have to work hard."

Alexis patted the baby's back, soft like a feather. The baby closed her eyes and went to sleep, still holding his shirt.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: Your nose can smell some things, like cookies baking, before you can see them.
story:
Aaron was at Grandma's house. He was playing with his blocks. Then he sniffed the air. Something smelled sweet.

"Grandma, I smell cookies!" he said.

Grandma smiled. "Your nose knows first," she said. "Follow the smell to the kitchen."

Aaron could not see the cookies yet. But his nose knew. He walked down the hall. The smell got bigger and bigger. He pushed the kitchen door open. There was Grandma, taking warm cookies from the oven with her big mitts.

"You found them," said Grandma. "Your nose found them before your eyes."

Aaron laughed. "Nose for smelling! Eyes for seeing!" Then he held up his hands. "Hands for touching." He touched a cool plate. He pointed to his ears. "Ears for hearing." Just then the phone did ring, and Grandma had to get it. Aaron waited for her answer, then clapped.

"Ears heard the phone!" he said.

"Right, not wrong," said Grandma. "And what is your mouth for?"

Aaron took a small bite of a cooled cookie. "Tasting!" he said. "Mmm. My nose found them. My mouth says thank you."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The counting words always go in the same order: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
story:
Jasper's class had ten toy cars. Jasper wanted to count them all. He lined them up on the rug. He touched each car. "One, two, three, four," he said. Then he stopped. He forgot what came next.

His friend Mia came over. Mia is in the big class. She has a big sister at home. Mia knelt down by the cars. She patted the fifth car. "Try again," she said. "One, two, three, four..."

Jasper looked at the cars. He touched them one by one. "One, two, three, four, five!" he said. His face felt warm and happy. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" All ten cars were counted. Miss Ella clapped from her chair. Jasper stood up and hugged the cars. "Ten cars," he said. Mia smiled. "You did it," she said.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: A scale at the doctor's office shows how much you weigh.
story:
Zoe went to the health clinic with her mom. The nurse had a friendly smile. "First we weigh you," she said.

Zoe stepped on the scale. She wiggled her toes. She bounced her knees. The numbers jumped up and down. "Why does it move?" Zoe asked. The nurse said, "Let's find out."

"Stand very still," Mom said. Zoe took a big breath. She stood still like a tree in the garden. The numbers stopped jumping. One number stayed. "That is how much you weigh," said the nurse.

"I did it!" said Zoe. Mom clapped.

Then it was time for Zoe's shot. Zoe squeezed her mom's hand. The nurse said, "Be still, just like on the scale." Zoe stood still. The shot was quick. It was done!

The nurse opened a drawer. She gave Zoe a shiny star sticker. Zoe stuck it on her shirt. "Can we come back?" Zoe asked. "Next year," said Mom, laughing.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: Breakfast is the first meal of the day.
story:
Jaxson ran into the kitchen in his pajamas. He opened the tall cupboard. He saw the cookie jar. "Cookies! Cookies for breakfast!" he called.

Mom shook her head. "Breakfast comes first," she said. "It is the very first meal of the day. Cookies are not breakfast."

Jaxson pouted. He wanted cookies. Mom held up two boxes. "You can pick," she said. "Eggs or oatmeal?"

Jaxson pointed at the eggs. Mom cracked them near the stove. Jaxson stood back and watched from his chair. The eggs sizzled and jumped. "The eggs are dancing!" he laughed.

Soon the plate was on the table. Jaxson took a big bite. "Yum," he said. "Eggs are my breakfast."

After breakfast, Jaxson had a bath. He got dressed in a tidy shirt. Then he asked, "Cookie now?"

Mom smiled. "Maybe after lunch, silly goose."

Jaxson whispered to the cookie jar, "Wait for me."

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: Shots help protect your body from getting some sicknesses.
story:
Zoe sat in the waiting room. She was not sick at all. Her nose was fine. Her tummy was fine. But the nurse said Zoe needed a shot today. Zoe hugged her teddy bear tight.

"Why do I need a shot?" Zoe asked. "I am not sick."

The nurse smiled a soft smile. "It helps protect your body," she said. "It keeps you from getting some sicknesses."

Zoe thought and thought. Then the nurse gave the shot in Zoe's arm. It felt like one tiny pinch. Zoe squeezed her teddy and it was done. The nurse put on a special blue bandage with stars.

After that, Zoe skipped down the hall with Mama. "Teddy needs a shot too," she said. She tapped his fuzzy arm. "There. Now he will stay well, just like me. We can go back to my class."

Zoe waved her star bandage at the door.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: Many drawing apps let you pick a colour by tapping it.
story:
Xavier sat at the little red table. Miss Ada put the tablet in front of him. "Can you turn it on?" she asked. Xavier pressed the big button. The screen lit up. He clapped his hands. He had made that happen!

Xavier wanted to draw. Miss Ada showed him the drawing app. He tapped it with one finger. A white page opened. Now he wanted a red sun. He looked at the colours at the top. He tapped blue. His finger made a blue line. "Not blue," said Xavier. "Sun is red."

His friend Mia leaned over. "Try the red one," she said. Xavier tapped the red circle. He drew a big round sun. It was red! He laughed and drew red rays all around it.

Then the teacher rang the bell. Time to clean up. Xavier pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He carried the tablet to the shelf, holding it with both hands like a bowl of soup. "Bye bye, sun," he said.
